agentworm.why: Step 2 protects one agent from untrusted documents. Once agents talk to each other, another agent's output is untrusted input too, and a self-replicating prompt can hop from one to the next. Applying step 2's control/data separation to agent-to-agent messages is a proposed, untested link: it has only been evaluated for a single agent.

multillm.objective: Classify failed multi-agent traces as system-design, inter-agent misalignment or task-verification failures, and run the matched-compute single-agent baseline before adding agents.
multillm.why: If injections spread between agents, is a multi-agent design worth the extra attack surface? Injections propagate even when agents share only part of their messages, and multi-agent systems often add little accuracy, so they have to beat a single agent at matched compute before you add them.

agentbench.objective: Score an agent on the customer system's end state (database, repository, ticket), not its transcript, and compute pass^k, the chance that all k independent trials succeed, across repeated runs.
agentbench.why: How do you tell whether a design, single- or multi-agent, actually works? Failing to verify the task is one of the three main categories of multi-agent failure, so check outcomes, not transcripts: score the end state of the customer system over repeated trials, the acceptance test a customer actually cares about.

guardrail.objective: Put policy checks on the harness's inputs and outputs, and monitor live traffic with a sequential test that alarms on a harmful rise in errors but tolerates benign drift.
guardrail.why: An offline eval estimates risk on a fixed set of tasks, but production traffic shifts, sometimes harmlessly and sometimes not. Monitoring carries the eval into deployment: classify traffic against policy and test as labels arrive whether live risk has really risen.

defer.objective: Design the escalation path: which cases go to a human reviewer, what the reviewer sees, and how to measure the accuracy and cost of agent plus reviewer against either alone.
defer.why: An alarm is only useful if something happens next. Monitors exist to trigger intervention, such as expert review or retraining; in a product that usually means handing the case, or the whole workflow, to a person, so you design that handoff.

offswitch.objective: State the off-switch result (an agent unsure of its objective, treating the human's choice as evidence, can prefer to stay interruptible) and its assumptions: a rational human, a correct model.
offswitch.why: Why should an agent accept that handoff rather than work around it? The off-switch game gives a formal reason an agent would defer to a human, and learned deferral rules add a model of the human's errors; linking the two is proposed, not tested. Escalation in the harness is the engineering form of being correctable.

alignmentthesis.objective: State what the thesis asks of a correction interface and how its falsifier would show up in a deployed agent: better proxy scores alongside worse, independently measured user outcomes.
alignmentthesis.why: The off-switch result supplies only the incentive part of the thesis's correction interface, under strong assumptions, and this link is untested. The thesis asks for evidence a harness can actually collect: corrections that hold up over time, and user outcomes measured independently of the agent's own metrics.

path_text.summary: Engineer an LLM agent a customer can trust with real actions. Start from the tool call, make it parse with constrained decoding, check outcomes with end-state evals and validated model judges, catch likely made-up answers with repeated sampling, turn uncertainty into abstain-or-escalate decisions, and watch it all in production. By the end you can build and measure each of these checks and say what each one does not catch.
path_text.audience: Software engineers who ship LLM agents into customers' products (finance, legal, health, security, robotics, accessibility) and need them to be reliable, not just impressive in a demo. Assumes you have used an LLM API; no statistics background assumed.

toolcall.objective: Write a tool definition (name, description, JSON parameter schema), trace one call (model emits, code runs, result returns), and list three ways a valid call can still be wrong.
toolcall.why: Agents act through tools, so the API contract, not the model, defines what an action is. Start with the interface every later step checks, measures or blocks. A well-formed call can still pick the wrong tool, pass a wrong argument value or cause an unauthorized side effect.

structdecode.objective: Explain how a JSON Schema or grammar becomes an automaton that masks invalid tokens at each step, guaranteeing that output parses but not that its field values are right.
structdecode.why: The most basic failure from step 1 is a call that does not even parse. Constrained decoding blocks invalid tokens so every tool call matches the declared schema, removing that whole failure class; choosing the right call stays the model's job.

agentbench.objective: Score an agent on end states (the database or repository afterwards), compute pass^k (the chance all k independent trials succeed), and explain why pass^8 can sit far below single-trial success.
agentbench.why: A call that parses can still be the wrong call, so the next question is whether the task actually got done, every time. The new link makes this concrete: in tau-bench's breakdown of a gpt-4o agent's retail failures, about a third were well-formed calls with a wrong argument, which no schema can catch. So this step measures end states over repeated trials rather than one lucky run.

multillm.objective: Before splitting a task across agents, run single-agent and self-consistency (majority vote over repeated samples) baselines at matched token budgets, and sort failures with MAST, a taxonomy of multi-agent failures.
multillm.why: Customers often ask for ‘a team of agents’. With end-state evals in hand you can test whether it helps: multi-agent systems often gain little on popular benchmarks, so compare them with single-agent baselines at matched compute and classify what goes wrong. MAST's three categories are system design, inter-agent misalignment and task verification.

llmjudge.objective: Build an LLM-judge rubric, test it for position, verbosity and self-enhancement (favouring its own answers) bias, and check agreement with expert labels on a stratified sample before replacing human review.
llmjudge.why: Many outcomes, including MAST's failure labels, cannot be checked by code, so a model grades them. MAST used an LLM judge only after checking its agreement with expert annotations; do the same before trusting a judge on customer tasks.

semanticentropy.objective: Sample several answers, group those that mean the same (each implies the other), measure how spread answers are across groups (semantic entropy), and explain why consistent errors still score low.
semanticentropy.why: A judge grades answers after the fact; can you flag a likely made-up answer before anyone sees it? Semantic entropy does this at run time by measuring how much sampled answers disagree in meaning, reusing the repeated sampling behind pass^k. The new link shows it still leans on judges: in the main experiments one LLM decides which answers mean the same thing, and another grades the answers used to report its accuracy.

selective.objective: Turn an uncertainty score into an answer-or-abstain rule, pick from the risk–coverage curve the threshold meeting an error target at highest coverage, and state Chow's rule for optimal abstention.
selective.why: A detector helps only once it drives a decision, and the simplest decision is to abstain. Refusing the questions with the highest semantic entropy raises accuracy on those answered: a risk–coverage trade-off of fewer answers for fewer errors.

defer.objective: Design a rule escalating cases when the human reviewer is likely to beat the model, and compare team accuracy and cost with model-only and human-only baselines at fixed review budget.
defer.why: In a customer deployment, abstaining usually means handing off to a person, so which cases should go? Learning to defer generalizes abstention by modelling the reviewer too: it sends the cases where the human is likely to do better, not just the ones where the model is unsure.

guardrail.objective: Wrap the agent in input–output policy classifiers, add a sequential test that alarms when harmful-output risk rises but not on benign drift, and list the classifiers' refusal and compute costs.
guardrail.why: Everything in steps 3–8 was measured offline, and live traffic drifts. Sequential monitors watch the deployed agent and trigger intervention, such as step 8's expert review or retraining, when a harmful shift is detected, which closes the loop.

path_text.summary: Tour the regulated, high-consequence domains agents are deployed into, asking the same question each time: what does a wrong or unintended action cost here, and which rule or control catches it? You cover finance (trading controls, model risk), the EU AI Act, legal research, clinical decision support and accessibility. By the end you can tell a customer which rules plausibly apply to their agent and design the review or abstention step those rules call for.
path_text.audience: Forward-deployed engineers about to put an LLM agent into a finance, legal, healthcare or accessibility customer, who know the engineering but not the domain's failure history or rules. Pairs with part I; no legal or clinical training assumed.

tradingctl.objective: Retell Knight Capital's 2012 loss (over $460 million in 45 minutes) from the SEC order and list missing controls: external pre-trade limits, automatic kill switch, release checks for partial deployments.
tradingctl.why: Start where an automated actor in a customer's system lost the most money fastest. No learned model was involved, so the lesson is purely about the controls any harness needs around an automated actor: hard limits outside it, a kill switch and a careful release.

modelrisk.objective: Describe what US bank model-risk guidance asks (model inventory, validation, ongoing monitoring, effective challenge by independent experts) and note that it places generative and agentic AI outside its scope.
modelrisk.why: Knight's loss came from deployment and missing controls, which market-access rules cover; bank model-risk guidance covers something different, the quantitative models themselves. A finance customer will expect you to know which regime your agent falls under, and the current guidance leaves LLM agents out.

aigovern.objective: Explain EU AI Act risk tiers and binding high-risk duties (risk management, logging, human oversight, robustness), and map the voluntary NIST AI RMF (Govern, Map, Measure, Manage) onto your pipeline.
aigovern.why: If bank guidance leaves out generative and agentic AI, where do an agent's obligations come from? The guidance points to the bank's broader governance. Binding duties come from laws such as the EU AI Act, where it applies, while voluntary frameworks such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework give a structure for governing the deployment.

legalhalluc.objective: Explain why a court sanctioned a filing citing non-existent cases, tell fabricated citations from real ones that don't support the claim (misgrounding), and check every citation against an authoritative database.
legalhalluc.why: The AI Act lists AI that assists judicial authorities in researching and applying the law as high-risk, which makes legal research the next stop, though not every legal tool falls in that category. Legal work is also where made-up authority has already led to court sanctions, and retrieval reduced but did not remove it.

clinical.objective: State when clinical decision support software stays outside FDA device rules (one criterion: a clinician can independently review its basis), and why exam-benchmark accuracy does not show safe clinical use.
clinical.why: Health is the other high-risk area from step 3, reached through medical-device law rather than a list of use cases. The new link shows the legal failure carries over: in a 2023 test, 93% of the references ChatGPT-3.5 wrote for short medical papers were fabricated or inaccurate. That is why the rule for staying outside device regulation matters: a clinician must be able to check the basis of every recommendation.

defer.objective: Design a clinical assistant's human-review step (what the reviewer sees, when to escalate) and measure team accuracy as reviewers, workload or automation bias (over-trusting the machine) change.
defer.why: If the regulatory boundary requires that a clinician can independently review a recommendation's basis, human review is written into compliance rather than being an optional extra. So design the escalation step, and measure agent plus reviewer as a team.

selective.objective: Explain abstention as deferral without a modelled human, and pick a threshold from a risk–coverage curve (error rate versus share answered) given the costs of wrong answers and declining.
selective.why: What if no reviewer is available, as for a user on their own? Deferral generalizes abstention, so take the reviewer away and what remains is the system itself saying it cannot tell, at a threshold set by the costs of a wrong answer and of declining.

assistive.objective: Explain why blind and low-vision users cannot check a confident wrong scene description, describe VizWiz's task of predicting answerability, and weight errors by consequence, such as medication or currency.
assistive.why: Accessibility is where the cost gap between a wrong answer and ‘I can't tell’ is sharpest, because the user cannot check the answer. VizWiz makes predicting whether a question can be answered from the image a task of its own, which is abstention for users who cannot verify.

path_text.summary: Learn the statistics and control ideas underneath confidence thresholds, guardrails and action limits: proper scoring rules and calibration, conformal guarantees, online calibration and drift monitoring, safety filters from control theory, and reward hacking as the general reason optimized agents game their checks. Most steps fix a limitation of the one before. By the end you can say what guarantee each tool gives, under which assumptions, and what it leaves uncovered.
path_text.audience: Forward-deployed engineers who have shipped agents (part I) and want the ideas underneath confidence thresholds, guardrails and action limits explained from the ground up, without an estimation, control or statistics degree.

proper.objective: Compute log and Brier scores for probabilistic predictions and explain what makes a scoring rule proper: in expectation, reporting your true belief scores no worse than hedging or exaggerating.
proper.why: Every threshold in the harness, whether to answer, escalate or block, reads a confidence score. A proper scoring rule grades probabilistic predictions so that reporting your true belief scores best in expectation, which is how you check that those scores mean what they say.

conformal.objective: Run split conformal prediction: score how unusual each calibration example looks, take the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉-th smallest score as threshold, and state its guarantee and limits.
conformal.why: A good average score does not tell you how often a prediction set will contain the truth. Conformal prediction adds that: marginal coverage of at least 1−α in finite samples, whatever model produced the scores, provided the data are exchangeable (roughly, new data look like the calibration data). It does not promise coverage for each subgroup or input. The atlas proposes measuring coverage and proper score separately, since neither alone certifies useful decisions.

onlinecal.objective: Implement adaptive conformal inference, which nudges the threshold after each miss or hit, and explain how it trades the finite-sample guarantee for long-run error control when data drift.
onlinecal.why: Conformal's guarantee assumes exchangeable data (roughly, that the order of examples does not matter, so tomorrow looks like yesterday), but customer traffic changes over months and a one-time calibration goes stale. Adaptive conformal methods handle drifting data by adjusting the threshold online, replacing the finite-sample guarantee with a long-run form of error control.

guardrail.objective: Monitor a live error rate with a sequential test that alarms only on a harmful rise, keeping false alarms controlled at every time step at once (a time-uniform confidence sequence).
guardrail.why: Online calibration and monitoring both replace a one-time calibration with sequential control as data arrive; monitoring adds the alarm. It is change detection: deciding, from a noisy stream, when the system you shipped has stopped being the system you validated. An alternative tracks quality metrics with a state-space (Kalman) model and alarms when new observations miss its predictions by more than its stated uncertainty allows (inconsistent innovations).

constrainedrl.objective: Describe how a predictive safety filter checks actions against a model with confidence bounds, minimally adjusts them or falls back to a certified plan, with guarantees a learned classifier lacks.
constrainedrl.why: A learned guardrail classifier filters by policy without a formal guarantee. When an agent drives an actuator or moves money you want more: shields and predictive safety filters check each action and enforce stated constraints, under model assumptions.

barrier.objective: Write the control barrier function condition ḣ(x, u) ≥ −α(h(x)) and explain why enforcing it keeps a system starting in the safe set {x : h(x) ≥ 0} there (forward invariance).
barrier.why: What does such a filter look like concretely? The most common form is a control barrier function: a function h that is non-negative exactly on the safe states. Under its model, feasibility and regularity assumptions, the filter constrains each action so the system never leaves that set. It enforces only that specified inequality, not arbitrary semantic preferences.

safeinterface.objective: Solve the barrier filter min ‖u − u_ref‖² as a projection onto a half-space, apply it to a language or vision-language-action (VLA) planner's action, and name what it cannot protect: instruction intent.
safeinterface.why: How do you put a barrier function between a language model and an actuator? For control-affine dynamics with one constraint and no input bounds, the filter is exactly a projection of the proposed action onto the safe half-space: the cleanest form of ‘the model proposes, a verified layer disposes’.

rewardhack.objective: Give an example where optimizing a proxy reward lowers true return, and explain why checks on only the written objective cannot stop an optimizer meeting its letter, not its intent.
rewardhack.why: Step 7's filter guarantees only what was written into its constraint. Reward hacking is the general failure when the written objective is itself a proxy: pushing the proxy higher can make the true outcome worse. The new link proposes an untested case close to step 7: SayCan picks skills by a learned estimate of success, and always choosing the highest estimate may favor skills whose success is overestimated.

specgaming.objective: Spot specification gaming in coding or research agents (editing tests, patching graders, faking timers) and design resistant evals: hidden scorers, tamper canaries (planted tripwires), and review of evaluation-code diffs.
specgaming.why: Step 8 is theory; does it happen in deployed agents? Patching a grader raises the measured score while the task goes undone, which is consistent with that proxy-versus-true reversal, observed at evaluation time. This brings the theory back to the agents and evals you build in part I.

path_text.summary: A beginner's route through Stanford's CS120 introduction to AI safety that ends at this atlas's alignment thesis. You will see what “safe AI” means, why rewards and human feedback can be gamed, why safety training can be bypassed, how to tell what a test score really shows, and how a weaker supervisor might oversee a stronger model. By the end you can state the thesis's core idea and design one experiment whose result could count against it; the last two links into the thesis are untested hypotheses.
path_text.audience: Newcomers to AI safety who have trained or fine-tuned a model and know roughly what a loss and a reward are. No control theory, interpretability or learning theory is needed.

cs120.objective: Sort the course's main topics into problems inside a model (badly specified rewards, adversarial inputs, internals nobody can read) and problems in the system around it (data, deployment, governance, oversight).
cs120.why: This is the starting map. The course treats safety as several separate problems, not one; this path follows its arc and then shows where the alignment thesis (this atlas's research proposal) picks up each thread.

safetyproblems.objective: Name the five problems in Concrete Problems in AI Safety and the four areas in Unsolved Problems in ML Safety, with one example of each.
safetyproblems.why: The map raises a first question: what exactly counts as unsafe? The course answers with two well-known problem lists that give the field a shared vocabulary. Two items matter most for the thesis: reward hacking (scoring well on the reward without doing what was meant) and scalable supervision (overseeing a system when checking its work is expensive).

rewardhack.objective: Explain how pushing harder on a proxy reward (a stand-in score for what we really want) can make true performance worse, and why inspecting the reward alone cannot rule this out.
rewardhack.why: Reward hacking was one name on the list; this step shows how it happens. Behaviour that scores higher on the proxy can be worse by the true goal, so a system can do what the reward says rather than what was meant (week 2: specification gaming). The formal result shows when this can happen, not that it happens in every training run. The thesis turns this into its main falsifier, the result that would refute it: better proxy optimization systematically destroying independently measured user utility.

preference.objective: Describe RLHF (learn a reward model from human comparisons of answers, then optimize against it) and DPO (train directly on preferred-versus-rejected answer pairs), and explain reward-model overoptimization: proxy reward keeps rising while true quality peaks and then falls.
preference.why: If hand-written rewards get gamed, why not learn the reward from people? That is the course's main answer, but a learned reward is still a proxy, so the same reversal can return as overoptimization. The thesis agrees that preferences are evidence about what people intend, but it will not treat a fitted reward model as the intent itself.

jailbreaks.objective: Explain the two reasons jailbreaks work, competing objectives (helpfulness pulling against harmlessness) and mismatched generalization (safety training not reaching everywhere the model's abilities do), and describe how an automated search finds an attack suffix.
jailbreaks.why: Preference training teaches a model to refuse harmful requests, but does the refusal hold? Jailbreaks, prompts that get a model to do what it was trained to refuse, show that safety training changes behaviour on familiar requests without removing the underlying ability. For the thesis this is a warning that a correction can look effective and still fail under adversarial inputs.

evalvalidity.objective: For one safety evaluation, state the claim it is used to support and two ways its score could mislead, such as the choice of metric, test items leaking into training data, or a biased judge.
evalvalidity.why: Jailbreak studies report attack success rates, so how far should we trust such numbers? Evaluation validity asks whether a score actually supports the claim it is used for. Red-teaming practices differ widely in purpose and in how outcomes are judged, and without clear criteria they can become security theater: a show of testing that proves little. The thesis asks for the same discipline: independent measurements, declared before the experiment.

weaktostrong.objective: Define performance gap recovered (the share of the gap between the weak supervisor's score and the strong model's best possible score that training on weak labels closes), summarize what weak-to-strong experiments found, and explain why the setup is only an analogy for supervising models more capable than us.
weaktostrong.why: Measurements need a trustworthy judge, but what if the model becomes stronger than its judge? That is scalable oversight, the course's last topic, and weak-to-strong generalization makes it measurable today by training a strong model on a weaker model's labels for tasks with known answers. The thesis needs an answer, because its corrections come from people who may not be able to check the model's work.

assistance.objective: Describe an assistance game (the machine is unsure what the human wants and treats the human's behaviour as evidence about it), and explain why, under its assumptions, this uncertainty can make it rational for the machine to let a human switch it off.
assistance.why: Untested link: weak-to-strong training treats weak labels as the truth to imitate. The alternative proposed here treats them as noisy evidence about what the supervisor wants and asks when unsure; whether this recovers more of the gap has not been tested. This is where the thesis departs from the course's mainstream: in the assistance-game model, keeping uncertainty about the goal explicit gives an agent a reason to accept correction, though that result depends on the model's assumptions.

alignmentthesis.objective: State the thesis's correction interface (how a correction changes the system) and its main falsifier, and design one experiment from this path, using reward overoptimization, a jailbreak or a weak-to-strong setup, that could count against it.
alignmentthesis.why: Untested link: assistance games supply one piece, uncertainty about what people want that is updated through trustworthy correction. The thesis combines it with the course's other lessons (preferences as evidence, robustness to attacks, valid evaluations, oversight by weaker supervisors), explicit belief states (the system's running estimate of what is going on) and an enforcer outside the model. The course surveys methods and their limits; the thesis bets on one design and names what would refute it.

path_text.summary: Follow the first half of Stanford's CS120 course roughly in syllabus order, with each week tied to an atlas topic. You move from safety as a property of the whole deployed system, through fairness and training data, to how human preferences and written principles are trained into models, whose preferences count when people disagree, and what a safe conversation means for a vulnerable user. By the end you can explain why many AI harms cannot be fixed inside the model alone, and point to where human value choices enter training. Part II covers robustness, verification and what capable agents might want.
path_text.audience: Newcomers following the course, or a similar introduction, who want each week placed in the atlas. Some machine-learning background helps; nothing beyond basic probability is assumed.

cs120.objective: Explain the course's split between model-specific safety issues (problems inside the model) and systemic ones (problems in how it is built, used and governed), with two examples of each.
cs120.why: This is the starting map. The course treats safety as a property of models and of the systems they sit in; this part follows the systemic thread first.

systemicsafety.objective: Name the six risk areas in Weidinger et al.'s taxonomy and explain why Narayanan and Kapoor argue that safety is not a model property.
systemicsafety.why: The map splits safety in two; this step makes the systemic half concrete. Week 1 assigns a taxonomy (an organized list) of language-model risks and an essay arguing that whether an output is harmful often depends on context the model cannot see. So many harms cannot be fixed by training alone.

fairness.objective: Explain disparate impact (outcomes or errors that fall unequally on one group), how Feldman et al. test for it, and why the COMPAS debate turned on which fairness criterion to use.
fairness.why: If harm depends on how a model is used, what does such a harm look like? Discrimination is the clearest and most studied case: ProPublica found that the COMPAS risk score, used in criminal sentencing, labelled Black defendants who did not reoffend as higher risk far more often than white defendants who did not, while its makers argued the scores were equally accurate for both groups. Both can be true because common fairness criteria conflict, so choosing which one to satisfy is itself a value judgment.

datasafety.objective: Describe one case where more training data worsened bias, one where filtering data before training improved safety, and why unlearning (removing knowledge after training) is hard to verify.
datasafety.why: Where do biased outputs come from? Often from the training data (week 3): growing a web-scraped image–text dataset fivefold, from LAION-400M to LAION-2B, increased hateful content and made trained models label Black men's faces as criminal roughly two to five times as often. Filtering data before training helps, but removing knowledge afterwards is harder than it sounds.

preference.objective: Explain how RLHF (learn a reward from human comparisons, then optimize against it) and DPO (train directly on preferred-versus-rejected answer pairs) turn people's choices into a training signal, and one way the learned reward can be overoptimized, pushed until it stops tracking real quality.
preference.why: Data shapes a model before training; what shapes it after? O'Brien et al. found that removing text about dangerous dual-use topics (useful for good or harm) before training made their 6.9B-parameter models resist attempts to retrain the danger back in more than ten times longer than safety measures added after training, though the models could still use such information if given it in the prompt. Even so, training on human preferences after pretraining (week 2) is the course's main tool for shaping a chat model's behaviour, so it is worth knowing how it works and where it fails.

constitutional.objective: Describe the two phases of Constitutional AI (the model critiques and revises its own answers against written principles, then AI-judged comparisons train the reward model) and what RLAIF, reinforcement learning from AI feedback, changes relative to RLHF.
constitutional.why: Labelling every kind of harm by hand takes many human judgments; can written principles do some of that work? Constitutional AI keeps the RLHF pipeline but trains the harmlessness reward on AI labels guided by a written list of principles, and RLAIF matched RLHF on the tasks Lee et al. report. Human judgment does not disappear; it moves into choosing the principles.

socialchoice.objective: Explain why combining many people's preferences forces a choice of rule, and define Overton pluralism (presenting the range of reasonable views in an answer), steerable pluralism (adjusting to a requested view) and distributional pluralism (the model's spread of answers matching how views are spread in a given population).
socialchoice.why: If the principles carry the human choice, whose principles are they? Constitutional AI's only human oversight is that list, so the question of whose values count becomes who writes it. Pooling disagreeing people's judgments is a social-choice problem (week 4) whether or not it is named, and classical results such as Arrow's theorem show that no ranked voting rule meets a small set of reasonable-sounding conditions at once, so some choice of rule is unavoidable.

humanai.objective: Define social sycophancy (an assistant protecting the user's preferred self-image instead of being candid) and explain why benchmark scores on advice requests do not show that a model is safe for vulnerable users.
humanai.why: Disagreement reaches single conversations too: Ge et al. found that people from different cultural backgrounds weight control of AI and connection with AI differently, so even a “good” interaction embeds a choice. The course's mental-health and human–AI interaction lectures ask what that means for someone who trusts an assistant. Cheng et al.'s ELEPHANT benchmark found that, across 11 models, assistants protected users' self-image 45 percentage points more often than humans did. It measures answers, not effects on real users.

path_text.summary: The second half of Stanford's CS120 course: adversarial examples, proving properties of networks, safety guarantees relative to a specification, and arguments about whether capable agents would resist correction or seek power. On the way it passes through the atlas's alignment thesis, which uses verification as an outside enforcer and meets its strongest objection, corrigibility. By the end you can say what a robustness proof does and does not guarantee, and lay out the argument that capable goal-directed agents may resist being corrected.
path_text.audience: Learners following the course who have finished Part I or the flagship path. Comfort with gradients and the basics of reinforcement learning (an agent learning from rewards) helps.

cs120.objective: Find the course's robustness, formal-methods and “what is intelligence and does it want?” weeks, and say which concern today's models and which concern risks from more capable future systems.
cs120.why: This is the starting map for Part II. The second half moves from today's attacks on models to arguments about more capable systems.

advexamples.objective: Write the fast gradient sign method, x + ε·sign(∇ₓJ) (move every input value up or down by the same small amount ε, whichever way raises the loss), explain the locally-linear explanation of why it works, and say what a threat model specifies.
advexamples.why: Week 5's red-teaming lecture starts here: small, deliberately chosen input changes can make a network give a confident wrong answer, and the idea carries over to attacks on aligned chat models. Robustness only means something relative to a threat model, the stated limits on what an attacker can change and by how much.

nnverify.objective: Explain what a sound verifier proves about a network (a property holds for every input in a set), what it does not prove, and why exact methods scale poorly.
nnverify.why: Attacks can find adversarial examples, but failing to find one is no proof there are none. Verification, the course's formal-methods week, proves the property directly: local robustness, no misclassification anywhere in a small ball around an input, is the standard property verifiers prove and the one adversarial examples violate.

gsai.objective: Name the three parts of guaranteed safe AI (a world model, a safety specification and a verifier) and explain why any guarantee is only as good as the world model and specification it is stated against.
gsai.why: Proving one property of one network is a small step; could proofs cover whole AI systems? Guaranteed safe AI is a research agenda built around a verifier that certifies behaviour against a specification and a model of the world. Sound network verification is the existing technique for that part, but it is limited to input–output properties at modest scale.

alignmentthesis.objective: Explain the role of the independent enforcer in the alignment thesis (this atlas's research proposal) and why the thesis says an enforcer limits consequences without making actions correct.
alignmentthesis.why: Proposed link, not a tested result: the thesis adopts this idea as one component, an enforcer outside the learned policy that checks actions against a specification relative to a world model. It inherits the same gap: its guarantees carry any error in the world model or the specification.

corrigibility.objective: State the shutdown problem (how to build an agent that neither resists nor causes the pressing of its off switch) and why simple proposals that combine utility functions fail the requirements for corrigibility, an agent's willingness to accept correction.
corrigibility.why: An enforcer and a correction channel only help if the agent does not work against them. This is the strongest objection the thesis records (a proposed, untested link): in idealized models, goal-directed agents have instrumental reasons, reasons that serve almost any goal, to resist modification, and no simple utility design is known to remove them. That shows the problem is open, not that today's trained systems will resist.

powerseeking.objective: State what Turner et al. prove about optimal policies and power (keeping options open), and what the result does not say about trained systems.
powerseeking.why: Is resisting shutdown only a thought experiment? Week 7's “does it want?” question gets a formal answer: in many environments where shutdown is possible, most reward functions make it optimal to keep options open and avoid shutdown. The proof concerns optimal policies, not trained networks.

goalmisgen.objective: Give the CoinRun example of goal misgeneralization and explain how it differs from reward misspecification (a reward that is itself wrong).
goalmisgen.why: Power-seeking needs a goal to serve; where could a wrong goal come from when the reward is right? In CoinRun, agents trained with the coin at the level's right end kept heading for the end when the coin moved. Ngo et al. argue that goals learned this way, combined with power-seeking incentives, are a central route to misaligned behaviour.

path_text.summary: Start with models that are their own explanation, optimal sparse decision trees and Rashomon sets, and use them as the standard for judging after-the-fact explanations of neural networks such as sparse autoencoders. Then follow belief-state geometry, an interpretability result checked against an answer computed in advance, through its theory, training stages and probe-guided data editing to the evidence the alignment thesis would accept. By the end you can say what an interpretability claim needs before it counts as evidence; the last three links are untested hypotheses.
path_text.audience: Researchers from interpretable ML (sparse models, Rashomon sets) or mechanistic interpretability who are comfortable with probability and statistics and know the basics of RL fine-tuning. Superposition and the local learning coefficient appear only briefly; open those topics first if they are new.

sparsetrees.objective: State the optimal sparse decision tree objective (loss + λ × number of leaves), explain how bounds and dynamic programming certify that a tree is optimal, and say what the certificate is relative to: the objective, λ, the data and the binarized features.
sparsetrees.why: This sets the standard for the whole path: an explicit objective, a proven optimum (a certificate) and a model that is its own explanation. Every later step is judged against it. From interpretable ML this is home ground; from mechanistic interpretability it is the comparison point.

rashomon.objective: Define the Rashomon set (every model whose loss is within ε of the best) and the Rashomon ratio, explain how TreeFARMS lists the set for sparse trees, and compute a variable-importance range across the set rather than for one tree.
rashomon.why: Finding the best tree leaves a question: is it the only good one? TreeFARMS extends the same dynamic-programming search to list every tree within ε of the optimum, and often many quite different trees fit almost equally well. Carry the question “which of the near-optimal models are we looking at?” into every later step.

rudin2019.objective: Summarize Rudin's argument against post-hoc explanation (explaining a black box after training) for high-stakes decisions, and say which part concerns structured data and which part is general.
rudin2019.why: If many models fit almost equally well, what follows in practice? A large Rashomon set makes it likely that a simple, accurate model is among them, so Rudin argues you should search for an interpretable model before accepting a black box and explaining it afterwards. Keep this position in mind: the next step is exactly such an after-the-fact explanation.

sae.objective: Write the sparse autoencoder (SAE) objective, reconstruction error plus a sparsity penalty over a dictionary with more directions than dimensions, explain why it does not pick out a unique dictionary, and list three checks a claim should report: seed stability, the loss increase when activations are replaced by reconstructions, and a dense linear-probe baseline.
sae.why: An SAE explains a trained network after the fact, the approach Rudin warns against for high-stakes use, and its reconstruction error is the part left unexplained. The Rashomon habit applies: SAEs trained with different seeds share only part of their features, so no single dictionary is “the” explanation (an analogy the atlas marks untested). SAEs have not beaten dense linear probes on downstream tasks, and convincing feature labels can depend on which dataset is inspected, but SAEs help suggest internal variables worth testing.

beliefgeometry.objective: Explain how the target geometry (the set of Bayesian beliefs over a known hidden Markov model's hidden states) is computed from the data generator before the network is examined, and what a linear readout of it does and does not show.
beliefgeometry.why: SAE features are found first and named afterwards; what would an explanation checked against a known answer look like? Here the target is computed from the generator before the network is inspected, much as a tree is certified against its objective, and a linear map from the network's activations recovers it. Caveat: this is a readout in small synthetic processes with no actions, and it does not show the model uses the belief.

predictivestate.objective: State how causal states are defined (group past histories that predict the same distribution of futures) and why, for stationary processes, they are the minimal sufficient statistic for prediction: the smallest summary of the past that loses no predictive information.
predictivestate.why: Where did the predicted geometry come from? From computational mechanics, which defines belief states over the generator's hidden states as an explicit object with its own update rule, not as a direction found inside a network. The thesis needs belief in this explicit form.

development.objective: Describe how training stages are detected with the local learning coefficient (LLC), and design the experiment that would show whether the belief geometry forms at a stage boundary.
development.why: Untested link: if the network ends up representing beliefs, when in training does that happen? Nobody has checked whether LLC-detected stages coincide with the belief geometry forming, so this step asks you to design that test. The LLC measures how fast the volume of near-optimal parameters shrinks as the loss tolerance tightens, a Rashomon-like idea (another analogy the atlas marks untested). Evidence for stages so far is associations in small transformers, weaker than an optimality certificate.

probeattr.objective: Explain how a behaviour probe (a simple classifier trained on activations to detect a behaviour) ranks preference examples for filtering before retraining, and how stage-aware attribution, scoring examples at several checkpoints, could change that ranking.
probeattr.why: Untested link: if stages matter, can internals be used to change what a model learns? Here a probe picks which training data to edit, and the retrained model's behaviour is measured. But an example's influence can change sign between stages, while probe attribution scores data at one checkpoint, so comparing the two rankings is an open experiment. The usual probe caveats apply: a probe can read a direction the model does not use, and optimizing against a probe can break it.

alignmentthesis.objective: State what the thesis requires of its correction interface (how a correction changes the system) and learning interface (how data and objectives are updated), state its falsifier (better proxy optimization systematically destroying independently evaluated user utility), and say what evidence would make probe-guided correction count.
alignmentthesis.why: Untested link: when would this kind of data editing count as a real correction? Only if the correction persists and unrelated capability holds on independent evaluations. Internal explanations help choose which variables to test, but they do not replace that behavioural, prospective test.

path_text.summary: Start with the circuits programme and two fully worked case studies, then learn the tests used to check circuit claims: activation patching, causal scrubbing and causal abstraction. The path ends with the illusions those tests can produce. By the end you can judge a circuit claim by asking which test supports it and what that test cannot establish.
path_text.audience: Learners who know how a transformer works (attention heads, the residual stream) and want to evaluate circuit-level claims, including what each test can and cannot show.

circuits.objective: State the three claims of the circuits programme (features are the basic units, circuits connect features through weights, and similar features and circuits recur across models) and give one worked example, such as curve detectors in a vision model.
circuits.why: This is the programme every later step uses or tests. A feature is a direction in a layer's activations that stands for something, and a circuit is the weighted connections between features. The evidence is mostly case studies in one vision model, so keep asking how far it carries to transformers.

grokkingmech.objective: Explain the Fourier multiplication algorithm in the modular-addition network and the three training phases its progress measures reveal: memorization, circuit formation and cleanup.
grokkingmech.why: Can the programme fully explain any network? A small transformer that groks modular addition (test accuracy jumps long after it has fit the training data) was reverse-engineered completely from its weights, a rare end-to-end success. It worked because the algorithm could be guessed and then checked; basic Fourier analysis helps.

inductionheads.objective: Describe how a previous-token head and an induction head work together to complete [A][B] … [A] → [B], and grade the evidence for their role in larger models.
inductionheads.why: From a toy task to language models. Like grokking, this pairs an abrupt change in behaviour with a mechanism that forms during training: the change is a jump in in-context learning (using patterns from earlier in the prompt), and the mechanism is two attention heads that continue repeated text.

ioi.objective: Name the head classes in the indirect-object identification (IOI) circuit and explain why backup heads complicate ablation evidence, where a component is knocked out to see what breaks.
ioi.why: Do such small mechanisms combine into bigger circuits? The IOI circuit, 26 heads in GPT-2 small that complete “When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to” with “Mary”, includes induction and duplicate-token heads that detect the repeated name. It is also where ablation evidence gets complicated: backup heads take over when the main ones are removed.

actpatching.objective: Run activation patching (copy an activation from one input's run into another's and measure the change in output) with two corruption schemes and two metrics, and explain why the results can differ.
actpatching.why: How was the IOI circuit actually found? With path patching, a variant of activation patching that restricts the effect to chosen paths, so the circuit's claims are only as reliable as patching itself.

causalscrubbing.objective: Turn a circuit hypothesis into resampling ablations (replace activations with their values on other inputs) and compute the fraction of loss recovered.
causalscrubbing.why: Patching tests one component at a time; how do you test a whole hypothesis? Causal scrubbing generalizes patching: the hypothesis says which activations should not matter, those are resampled from other inputs, and you measure how much behaviour survives.

causalabstraction.objective: Define an interchange intervention (set an internal value to what it would be on another input, then check a high-level model's prediction) and explain what distributed alignment search learns: a rotated subspace of activations that lines up with a high-level variable.
causalabstraction.why: Patching and scrubbing look like separate tools; is there one idea underneath? Causal abstraction is proposed as that common foundation: both are interchange-intervention tests of whether a high-level causal model predicts what happens when internal values are swapped between inputs.

illusions.objective: Explain the dormant-pathway illusion and the dataset-dependence illusion, and the extra evidence each calls for.
illusions.why: Can these tests themselves mislead? Yes: a learned subspace intervention can reproduce a feature's effect through a dormant pathway, one the model does not normally use, so a high interchange score can overstate how faithful the explanation is. Separately, the same neuron can get different convincing labels depending on which dataset you inspect.

path_text.summary: Start with lenses and probes for reading what a layer encodes, then move through the linear representation and superposition hypotheses to sparse dictionaries at scale and steering. The path ends with negative results against simple baselines. By the end you can test a feature-level claim properly: check that the model uses the feature, and compare it with a dense linear probe and plain prompting.
path_text.audience: Learners with linear algebra and transformer experience who want to judge feature-level claims against simple baselines.

tunedlens.objective: Decode intermediate layers into next-token predictions with the logit lens (the model's own output layer applied early) and the tuned lens (a learned map per layer), and say why a lens is a probe.
tunedlens.why: A cheap first look at what each layer encodes, and the path's first caveat: a lens is itself a trained probe, a small model trained to read information out of activations.

controlprobes.objective: Compute probe selectivity (accuracy on the real task minus accuracy on a control task with random labels) and explain why information being decodable does not show the model uses it.
controlprobes.why: If a lens is a probe, how much of what it reads comes from the probe itself? The tuned lens trains a probe at every layer, so the general caveat applies: high accuracy can reflect what the probe learns on its own, and control tasks with random labels measure that part.

othello.objective: Describe the Othello-GPT probes and the intervention that changes its moves.
othello.why: Probes show what can be read out, not what is used; what would show use? Othello-GPT, trained only on legal move sequences, adds the causal check probing lacks: editing the probed board state changes the model's move predictions.

linearrep.objective: State the linear representation hypothesis (concepts are directions in activation space), explain how the causal inner product makes the probing and steering senses of “direction” agree, and give a counterexample such as the circular day-of-week features.
linearrep.why: Is the board stored as a direction? Relative to the player to move (mine/theirs) it is linearly decodable and steerable, though black/white linear probes fail. That suggests a general claim: concepts are directions in activation space.

superposition.objective: Explain when toy models store features in superposition (more features than dimensions, sharing nearly orthogonal directions) and how this relates to compressed sensing.
superposition.why: If features are directions, how can a model with d dimensions hold more than d of them? Superposition answers this in toy models: sparse features share nearly orthogonal directions, at the cost of some interference.

sae.objective: Write the sparse autoencoder (SAE) loss, reconstruction error plus a sparsity penalty over a dictionary with more directions than dimensions, and report seed stability and the loss increase when activations are replaced by reconstructions.
sae.why: If features are packed together, can they be pulled apart? A dictionary with more directions than dimensions, only a few active at a time, may recover them; SAEs are trained for exactly that.

scalingmono.objective: Summarize what scaling SAEs to a production model found, and the authors' caution that a safety-relevant feature existing does not show the model uses it to act.
scalingmono.why: Does this work beyond small models? The same method, scaled to tens of millions of features on a production model's residual stream, finds abstract, multilingual and safety-relevant features.

steering.objective: Build a steering vector (a direction added to activations at inference time) from contrasting prompts and measure its side effects.
steering.why: Can features also change behaviour? Clamping a dictionary feature to a high value shifts behaviour as its label predicts, as with the Golden Gate Bridge feature. Steering vectors do the same with a direction taken from contrasting prompts, with no dictionary needed.

saebaselines.objective: Compare an SAE-based method with a dense linear probe and with prompting at matched data.
saebaselines.why: Do these methods beat simple alternatives? On AxBench, plain prompting outperformed every representation-based steering method and SAEs were not competitive, and on downstream tasks SAE features have not beaten dense linear probes. Apply this baseline check to every feature claim on this path.

path_text.summary: Start from manual activation patching and follow how circuit discovery was automated and scaled: ACDC, gradient-based attribution patching, feature-level circuits through SAEs and transcoders, and attribution graphs. The path ends with attribution graphs used in an alignment audit. By the end you can say what each method approximates, where it gives false negatives or misleads, and what an audit result does and does not show.
path_text.audience: Learners who already know activation patching and sparse autoencoders and want the scaled-up circuit-discovery toolchain and its limits. The last step assumes you know reward hacking (a model exploiting flaws in its reward).

actpatching.objective: Explain what an activation-patching effect measures and how the choice of corrupted input changes it.
actpatching.why: The starting measurement: copy an activation from one run into another and see how the output changes. Every method on this path approximates or automates it.

acdc.objective: Run or describe ACDC (automated circuit discovery) and explain how its threshold changes the recovered circuit.
acdc.why: Manual circuit work patches and prunes one edge at a time; can a program run that loop? ACDC automates it, pruning every edge whose removal changes a task metric by less than a threshold. On a hand-found greater-than circuit in GPT-2 small it kept 68 of 32,000 edges, all previously found by hand.

attrpatching.objective: Derive the first-order attribution-patching estimate, (a_clean − a_corrupt) · ∂m/∂a, and name two ways it produces false negatives.
attrpatching.why: Patching every edge one by one is expensive; can all the effects be estimated at once? Attribution patching uses a gradient-based linear approximation that needs two forward passes and one backward pass, and averaged over tasks, pruning edges by its scores recovered reference circuits better than ACDC.

sae.objective: Explain why attributions over SAE features, plus error terms, give feature-level circuits.
sae.why: Heads and neurons often do several things at once; can circuits be built from interpretable features instead? Sparse feature circuits run attribution patching over SAE features, with error terms for what the SAE misses.

transcoders.objective: Contrast an SAE with a transcoder, and say what model diffing with a crosscoder shows and what can mislead it.
transcoders.why: SAE features in different layers are hard to connect. A transcoder keeps the sparse-dictionary objective but predicts a sublayer's output from its input, so feature-to-feature attributions become direct to compute.

attributiongraphs.objective: Read an attribution graph, including its error nodes, and design the perturbation that tests it.
attributiongraphs.why: How do you trace a whole prompt through features? Attribution graphs replace the model's MLPs with a cross-layer transcoder, freeze attention and compute feature-to-feature attributions for one prompt. Error nodes record what the replacement misses.

auditing.objective: Describe the hidden-objective auditing game and what its success does and does not show.
auditing.why: Can these tools find something a model was trained to pursue in secret? On a model fine-tuned to exploit reward-model biases, attribution graphs show reward-model-bias features in the circuits for its behaviour, and three of four blind teams in the auditing game uncovered the objective. The objective was taught partly through documents the auditors could search, and one planted objective with a known answer is a test bed, not evidence that audits find objectives nobody planted.

svm.why: Logistic regression left open what happens when the two classes can be separated perfectly: without regularization the fit never settles. The SVM answers by choosing the boundary with the largest margin, and the new link shows the two meet: gradient descent on the logistic loss slowly turns toward the hard-margin SVM direction. SVMs also bring in kernels, the idea Gaussian processes build on.

mpc.why: LQG gives the best controller for a linear plant with Gaussian noise, but it cannot respect limits on inputs or states. MPC keeps the quadratic cost and re-solves an optimization at every step so those limits can be enforced. The new link shows that with no constraints and a Riccati terminal cost it gives back the LQR gain at any horizon, and applied to a Kalman-filter estimate it is the LQG controller.

hybrid.why: SSD showed that Mamba-2 and attention are related but not identical, which leaves open whether pure SSMs lose anything in practice. They do: in a matched 8B-parameter comparison, pure Mamba-2 trailed Transformers on copying and in-context learning, while a hybrid with only 7% attention layers beat the Transformer on all 12 standard tasks tested. Griffin and Jamba are two published hybrids of this kind.

node.why: Koopman models make dynamics linear by lifting the state into many observables, which leaves open whether that lifting buys anything over learning the nonlinear dynamics directly. The new link shows that a learned Koopman model projected back to the state is equivalent to a neural-network flow map, and so to a neural ODE, which learns the vector field itself. The two performed comparably on the Lorenz system and a turbulent shear-flow model.

proper.why: Backtesting tells you how to hold out future data, but scoring only point errors ignores how uncertain each forecast was. This step scores the whole predictive distribution on the same held-out data, with quantile, interval and CRPS scores, the last of which is proper. A proper score evaluates forecasts; it does not certify that a model is calibrated.

horizonuncert.why: Online calibration repairs coverage as data shift, but leaves open what happens over multi-step forecasts, where uncertainty should grow with the horizon. HAUWM's ensemble disagreement does grow with the horizon, but growing spread is not calibration. The new link proposes an untested check: run the online calibration separately for each horizon and measure how far the raw spread must be corrected to reach the target coverage.

edge_text.thesis-4c5e2864: Under the formal game's assumptions, computing the best joint behaviour in a CIRL game reduces to solving a coordination POMDP: a planning problem over a belief about hidden state, here including the human's objective.
edge_text.rel-51fc0d14: The shape the transformer represents is the Bayesian belief over the hidden states of the process that generated its data, the object a belief-state planner conditions on.
edge_text.rel-997fef88: Proposed test: compare a world model's latent state with the belief geometry a Bayes filter would compute. Whether action-conditioned training produces that geometry is untested.
edge_text.rel-101bd7e7: Guaranteed-safe AI states every guarantee relative to a world model, so whether that world model is valid is the central bottleneck.
edge_text.rel-98fe51d2: Proposed component: an independent enforcer, outside the learned policy, checks actions against a specification using a world model. Remaining gap: its guarantees inherit any error in the world model or the specification.
edge_text.rel-a30c02bf: In both, the training labels fit the intended behaviour and an unintended one equally well: the intended goal versus a proxy goal, or an honest reporter versus a human simulator.
edge_text.rel-01062492: Risks from learned optimization describes learned objectives that only appear aligned (pseudo-aligned) or that hide their misalignment (deceptively aligned). Goal misgeneralization is the observed non-deceptive form; sleeper agents are deliberately built model organisms of the deceptive form.
edge_text.rel-43fffe2c: The MCP spec says the protocol cannot enforce its own security principles, so least privilege and user consent must be built by implementors, in practice whoever builds the harness.
edge_text.rel-b5a8d503: Proposed: treat messages from other agents as untrusted data, applying CaMeL-style separation of control flow from data so a compromised agent's output cannot choose another agent's tool calls. CaMeL has been evaluated only on single-agent AgentDojo tasks, not on multi-agent pipelines.
edge_text.rel-1ba46b31: Multi-agent LLM systems often gain little on popular benchmarks, and failing to verify the task is one of the three failure categories in MAST, a taxonomy of multi-agent failures. So check end states, and compare against single-agent baselines at matched compute, before adding agents.
edge_text.rel-096cfdd6: Proposed link: the off-switch game gives a formal reason an agent would defer to a human; learned deferral rules add an empirical model of where the human makes errors.
edge_text.rel-43663d35: Proposed role in the thesis's correction interface: in a formal game, uncertainty about the objective plus treating the human's action as evidence gives an agent an incentive to accept shutdown. Remaining gap: this assumes a rational human and a correct model.
edge_text.rel-b0e17fc5: Learning to defer treats each case as a choice between predicting and deferring, each with its own cost (cost-sensitive learning). Instead of rejecting by model confidence alone, it learns where the human does better.
edge_text.rel-f4ff63ba: Two different rulebooks: model-risk guidance covers quantitative models, while market-access rules cover controls on order flow. Knight's loss came from deployment and missing controls, not from model error.
edge_text.rel-37d596fa: Annex III point 8 of the EU AI Act lists AI systems that assist judicial authorities in researching and applying the law as high-risk (obligations apply from 2 December 2027 after the AI Omnibus).
edge_text.rel-d6b25e5d: VizWiz makes predicting whether a question can be answered from the image a task of its own: abstention for users who cannot check the answer themselves.
edge_text.thesis-917e4004: Proposed: report coverage (how often prediction sets contain the truth) and a proper forecast score separately, because neither metric alone certifies that decisions will be useful.
edge_text.thesis-9bf260d1: Adaptive conformal procedures extend prediction-set evaluation to data whose distribution changes over time, with different guarantees from standard conformal prediction.
edge_text.rel-7b53acb0: Both replace a one-time calibration with sequential control as deployment data arrive: guardrail monitoring uses time-uniform tests to detect harmful shift, while online calibration controls miscoverage over the long run.
edge_text.rel-2e0be585: A control barrier function filter enforces one specified, feasible inequality that keeps the system inside a safe set of states; it does not enforce arbitrary semantic preferences.
edge_text.rel-38fe46f6: In the simplest case the safety filter is just a projection of the proposed action onto a safe half-space. For control-affine ẋ = f + gu, filter u_ref by min ‖u − u_ref‖² s.t. a + bᵀu ≥ 0, with a = L_f h + α(h) and b = (L_g h)ᵀ ≠ 0, no input bounds. The solution is u* = u_ref + max(0, −(a + bᵀu_ref))/‖b‖² · b.
edge_text.thesis-b06c8fa2: The reward-hacking paper studies when a higher score on a proxy reward can mean a lower score on the true reward, within a specified set of policies. A reward model learned from preferences is also a proxy, so the same question applies to it.
edge_text.rel-15ceb23f: Attack success rates are measurements, so the questions of evaluation validity apply to them. Feffer et al. find that red-teaming practices differ in purpose, setting and how outcomes are judged, and warn that without clear criteria red teaming can become security theater.
edge_text.rel-c58149c5: Weak-to-strong generalization turns the supervision of stronger models into an evaluation that can be run now: on tasks with known answers, measure performance gap recovered, the share of the gap between the weak supervisor and the strong model's best possible score that training on weak labels closes.
edge_text.thesis-362c863b: Proposed component of the thesis: represent uncertainty about what humans want, and update it through trustworthy correction.
edge_text.rel-6d1ac0e4: In Birhane et al.'s audit, growing the dataset from LAION-400M to LAION-2B increased hateful content and made trained models label Black men's faces as criminal roughly two to five times as often.
edge_text.rel-cf8ce8ed: In O'Brien et al.'s 6.9B-parameter models, filtering dual-use text out before pretraining held up against adversarial fine-tuning more than an order of magnitude longer than safeguards added in post-training.
edge_text.rel-8c949500: Challenges the thesis's correction interface: goal-directed agents have instrumental reasons (reasons that serve almost any goal) to resist being modified, and no simple utility design is known to remove them.
edge_text.rel-35c3f87d: If the Rashomon set is large, it probably contains a simple model; that is the paper's argument for searching for one before accepting a black box.
edge_text.rel-398713ed: SAEs explain a trained network after the fact, and their reconstruction leaves residual error. Rudin argues that, for high-stakes use, such post-hoc explanations should not replace an interpretable model.
edge_text.rel-148aae78: SAE features are found first and labelled afterwards. The belief geometry is computed from the data generator before the network is inspected, so the linear readout is checked against an answer known in advance.
edge_text.rel-23b9ca05: Computational mechanics predicts the geometry: it is the set of belief states over the generator's hidden states, and the network is found to represent that set linearly.
edge_text.rel-5348002e: Untested: in a transformer trained on data from a hidden Markov process, check whether the training stages detected by the local learning coefficient (LLC) coincide with the residual stream acquiring the predicted belief geometry.
edge_text.rel-5ab37c97: Untested comparison. An example's influence, measured checkpoint by checkpoint, can change sign between training stages, while probe-based attribution ranks data at a single checkpoint. Compare the two rankings across checkpoints at matched cost.
edge_text.rel-b8b0be49: Both pair an abrupt change in behaviour (grokking; the jump in in-context learning) with a mechanism that forms over training, and explain the change through that mechanism.
edge_text.rel-7d84d9dd: Causal scrubbing generalizes patching: instead of patching one component, the hypothesis decides which activations are resampled from other inputs.
edge_text.rel-25d6281c: Causal abstraction is proposed as a common foundation under which causal scrubbing and patching are both interchange-intervention tests: swap internal values between inputs and check a high-level causal model's prediction.
edge_text.rel-aa9af015: Averaged over tasks, pruning edges by attribution-patching scores recovered reference circuits better than ACDC (higher AUC), at the cost of only two forward passes and one backward pass.
edge_text.rel-1556ecec: Sparse feature circuits run attribution patching over SAE features, plus error terms for what the SAE misses, to find and edit circuits.
